1240.title: On the Incarnation
1240.hook: Athanasius, at about twenty-five, explains why the Word became flesh
1240.howItsDone: Christians confess in the Nicene Creed that the Son of God was incarnate and made man; churches celebrate the Incarnation at Christmas and the Annunciation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Origen's search: scripture as body, soul and spirit, read as a climb. Your line was read upward.

A great king enters a great city and moves into one house on one street. Just one. And yet, the story goes, the whole city is honored. Robbers who had been circling it lose their nerve, because the king lives there now. That small parable comes from a short book by Athanasius, who became bishop of Alexandria. The book asks a question at the center of the Christian story: why would God's Word become a human being? Its title is today's word: On the Incarnation.

Athanasius starts with a problem. People were made in God's image, made from nothing and held in being by God. But turning from God, they were sliding back toward nothing: toward death and decay. And God, he says, couldn't simply watch his own work fall apart. That would be unworthy of God. Here he gives a second picture. A portrait painted on wood has been ruined, smeared until the face is gone. The painter doesn't throw away the board. The person in the portrait comes back and sits again, so the likeness can be redrawn on the same wood. That, for Athanasius, is the Incarnation. The Word of God came and took a body like ours, so the image could be restored from inside humanity, and death undone by his rising. Paul has a line for the coming down: Christ "took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men." Now the king in the city makes sense. By living in one human body, the Word honored every human body, and the powers that preyed on us lost their grip. Near the end of the book, Athanasius says it in one breath, here in paraphrase: he became human so that we might be made divine. Orthodox Christians call that sharing theosis. Catholics and some Protestants speak of it in the words of Second Peter: "partakers of the divine nature." Churches describe it differently. Athanasius's starting point is plain enough: God didn't stay far away.

Think of one thing in your own life that feels smeared or ruined, and let the picture sit beside it without forcing anything: the wood isn't thrown away, it's kept and worked on. If you pray, you can offer it to God as it is.

1241.title: The Cappadocians
1241.hook: Basil and the two Gregorys gave the words for three persons in one being
1241.howItsDone: Churches confess one God in three persons in the Nicene Creed, baptize in the name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and close prayers and blessings by naming all three; Orthodox and Catholic churches honor Basil and the two Gregorys as saints and teachers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, On the Incarnation: Athanasius and the portrait redrawn on the same wood. Your line was a king in the city.

Ask the money-changer for change, and he lectures you about the Begotten and the Unbegotten. Ask the baker the price of bread, and he tells you the Father is greater and the Son is less. Ask whether the bath is ready, and the attendant informs you that the Son was made from nothing. That's Gregory of Nyssa, in a sermon, complaining about a great city where everyone seemed to have an opinion about God. The arguments over the Trinity weren't happening only in libraries. They were happening at the market. Today, the people who sharpened the church's words: the Cappadocians.

Cappadocia is a region in what is now central Turkey. From there came Basil of Caesarea, his brother Gregory of Nyssa, and their friend Gregory of Nazianzus. Gregory of Nyssa also wrote about their sister Macrina as a teacher in her own right. The question they faced was old; this path first met it on day two hundred ninety-nine. Jesus sends his disciples out baptizing "in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost." One name, three named. So is God one or three? The Cappadocians answered with two Greek words, and gave each a separate job. Ousia, being: what God is. There is one. Hypostasis, person: who God is. There are three, Father, Son and Holy Spirit. One being, three persons. Not three gods working as a team. Not one God wearing three masks. They offered comparisons, like three people sharing one human nature, and then warned that every comparison falls short, because God is not one more thing in the world. Gregory of Nazianzus put the experience of it this way, in paraphrase: no sooner do I think of the One than I'm lit up by the Three; no sooner do I tell the Three apart than I'm carried back to the One. Their words helped shape how the Nicene Creed came to be understood. For them, the Trinity was not a puzzle to solve. It was a mystery to stand inside.
screen: `LIT BY THE THREE, BACK TO THE ONE.`

If you pray, say it slowly, letting each name land, grace, love, communion; if you don't, just listen to the shape of it, three names, one blessing, given to everyone at once.

1242.title: Augustine's Confessions
1242.hook: a book about a life, written the whole way through as a prayer to God
1242.howItsDone: Christians of different churches read Augustine's Confessions as a spiritual classic, and some keep a prayer journal in the same spirit, writing to God directly about their lives.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Cappadocians: Basil and the two Gregorys, finding words for one God in three persons. Your line was three and one.

A teenager and his friends climb into a neighbor's orchard at night and strip a pear tree. They aren't hungry; they have better pears at home. They take a bite or two and throw the rest to the pigs. You met those pears back in year three. Years later, the thief is a bishop named Augustine, and he can't stop asking why he did it. His uncomfortable answer: because it was forbidden, and because his friends were there. The story sits in a book called the Confessions, and here's the strange part. It isn't written to us. Page after page, it's written to God.

The Confessions open with praise, borrowing a psalm: great is the Lord, and greatly to be praised. Then comes the sentence that holds the whole book. In Pusey's old translation, Augustine says to God: "for Thou madest us for Thyself, and our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee." That's the map. The rest is Augustine telling how restless he was. He chased learning, success, and applause as a teacher of speech. He chased love, and loved badly. He tried one philosophy after another. Each, he says, was a place he hoped to rest, and none of them held. The word confession does two jobs here. It means owning up: the pears, the pride, the people he hurt. And it means praise: confessing who God is. Augustine does both in the same breath, so the book reads like one long conversation, him talking and listening for an answer. The turn comes in a garden in Milan. He's weeping under a fig tree, sick of himself, when he hears a child's voice from a nearby house, chanting: "Take up and read; Take up and read." He opens the letters of Paul where they fall, and reads: "put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make not provision for the flesh." He says the shadows of doubt fled away. Christians in different churches, Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant, still read the Confessions. Some come for the conversion. Some come for the honesty: a bishop, writing down that he stole fruit to impress his friends.

Write one short paragraph to God, the way Augustine does, or, if you don't pray, a letter you're not sure where to send. Say one true thing about where you are today: what you're chasing, what you're tired of, what you're glad of. Don't polish it; Augustine didn't hide the pears.
Augustine's Confessions. The story of a restless life, told as a prayer: owning up to what he did, and praising the God he says he was looking for all along.
Your line: our heart is restless. Augustine's whole book hangs on it. Rest well.

1243.title: Lover, beloved, love
1243.hook: Augustine's picture of the Trinity from human love
1243.howItsDone: Christians speak of the Trinity as the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, one God, and some preachers and teachers in the Western churches use Augustine's picture of lover, beloved and love to describe it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Augustine's Confessions: a stolen pear, a garden, a child's voice saying take up and read. Your line was our heart is restless.

A grandmother kneels in a hallway, teaching a small boy to tie his shoe. Loop, swoop, pull. He gets it wrong, she laughs, and they start again. Count what's in that hallway. Her, the one loving. Him, the one being loved. And something else, not a third person exactly, but real enough that anyone walking past would see it: the love itself, running between them. Augustine, the same restless bishop from yesterday, wrote a long book on the Trinity, the teaching you first met in year one. Partway through, he stops at this very thing: love.

His starting point is a short line in the first letter of John: "for God is love." Augustine takes it seriously. If God is love, what does love need? Someone who loves. Someone who is loved. And the love itself. Lover, beloved, love: three, and yet one thing happening. In his book on the Trinity, he says that if you see love, you see the Trinity. Some readers map it this way: the Father as the one who loves, the Son as the one loved, the Spirit as the love that binds them; Augustine himself ties the Spirit closely to love. In John's Gospel, Jesus prays to the Father: "thou lovedst me before the foundation of the world." Love between the Father and the Son, older than the world. Here's what's honest about Augustine. He doesn't call the picture done. He says it's a beginning, a place to rest a moment, and keeps climbing. He turns inward, to the human mind: the mind, its knowing of itself, its love of itself. Later he tries memory, understanding and will. And near the end of the book he admits that every picture he's tried falls short of God. Christians weigh these images differently. Western theologians have drawn on them; some Orthodox theologians prefer to begin where the Cappadocians did, from the three persons. Augustine never claimed his picture was the whole thing. He offered it as a window, small and human: love needs more than one to be love.

Bring to mind two people you've seen love each other well: a parent and a child, a couple at a bus stop, two old friends laughing at the same joke one more time. Notice the one giving, the one receiving, and then the thing between them that belongs to neither alone, and stay with that third thing. If you pray, you can thank God for it.
Lover. In Augustine's picture of the Trinity, love needs three things to be love: the one who loves, the one who is loved, and the love itself.
Your line: love in three. Augustine called it a window, not the whole view. See you tomorrow.

1244.title: Boethius in prison
1244.hook: condemned and waiting, he writes the Consolation of Philosophy, where Lady Philosophy comes to his cell
1244.howItsDone: Christian readers have turned to Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy in times of loss, and the image of Fortune's wheel appears in Christian art, poetry and preaching.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Augustine's picture of love: lover, beloved, and the love between them. Your line was love in three.

A man sits in confinement, writing sad poems. Not long ago he was a powerful official at the king's court. Now, as he tells it in his own book, he's condemned, his good name gone, and he's waiting. The Muses of poetry stand around his bed, feeding him lines of grief. Then a woman appears above his head, her robe old and torn, as if rough hands had ripped pieces away. She sends the Muses packing, sits on the edge of his bed, and wipes his eyes with a fold of her dress. He knows her. She's Philosophy. This is Boethius in prison.

The book is the Consolation of Philosophy, a conversation between a broken man and the wisdom he had studied all his life. Philosophy doesn't start with comfort. She starts with diagnosis: you've forgotten who you are. Then, in the second book, comes an image: Fortune's wheel. In one passage Philosophy speaks in Fortune's own voice. I turn a wheel, Fortune says. I bring the low up and the high down. Climb on if you like, but don't call it unfair when it brings you down again; that's the game you agreed to play. Change isn't Fortune betraying you. Change is what Fortune is. So Philosophy asks Boethius to look at what he's lost: money, office, applause. Were they ever really his? What can be taken away was only on loan. What can't be taken is the good itself, and Philosophy leads him, step by step, toward God as that highest good, the still center the wheel turns around. Boethius was a Christian who wrote on the Trinity, yet this book never names Christ. The help comes from reason. Christian readers have still treasured it, hearing echoes of scripture. Hannah's song in First Samuel: "The LORD maketh poor, and maketh rich: he bringeth low, and lifteth up." And Job, stripped of everything: "the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD."

Picture a wise friend on the edge of your bed, the way Philosophy sat with Boethius, asking what this took that was only on loan, and what's still yours; if you pray, bring both answers to God. If a loss ever feels too heavy to carry alone, or you're thinking of harming yourself, call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.

1245.title: The ladder of names
1245.hook: Dionysius the Areopagite: God beyond names, beyond being
1245.howItsDone: Eastern Orthodox Christians in particular speak of the apophatic way, approaching God by saying what God is not; Christians of different churches practice wordless prayer in the same spirit.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Boethius in prison, and Philosophy at the edge of his bed. Your line was the wheel turns.

At the end of a chapter in Acts, after a speech, comes a short list of the people who stayed behind: "Howbeit certain men clave unto him, and believed: among the which was Dionysius the Areopagite, and a woman named Damaris, and others with them." That's all the Bible tells us about him. A name in a list. The speech had started from an altar with no god's name on it, and Paul read its inscription aloud: "TO THE UNKNOWN GOD. Whom therefore ye ignorantly worship, him declare I unto you." Later, writings appeared under his name that go straight back to that altar, asking whether not knowing God's name could be where wisdom starts.

The texts claim the name of that listener from Acts. Modern scholars generally read them as written much later by an unknown author, and call him Pseudo-Dionysius; Orthodox tradition still honors them under the name Dionysius. What they teach is a ladder that runs two ways. Going down, you name God. Scripture gives plenty of names: good, light, life, wisdom, love. In The Divine Names, Dionysius treats them one by one, and says each is true. God really is good. God really is light. Then the climb back up runs the other way: you take the names off, starting from the lowest. God is not a rock, not a fire, not a king the way kings are kings. Keep climbing, and even the high names come off. God is not good the way we know good, not even being the way things are. Not because God is less, but because God is beyond. Dionysius says God is both the one with many names and the nameless one. At the top there's no more talking. He points to Moses on the mountain: "Moses drew near unto the thick darkness where God was." A darkness, Dionysius says, that's actually too much light. This way of speaking is called apophatic: speaking of God by saying what God is not. Eastern Orthodox theology makes much of it, and Western mystics drew on it too. It gave Christians a humility in words: every name is true, and every name falls short.
screen: `UP THE LADDER: TAKE THE NAMES OFF.`

segments.voice: If you pray, say one name you use for God, Father, Lord, light, love, slowly, inside; if you don't, choose a word for whatever is biggest to you. Then let even that word go quiet, and stay in the space it pointed toward without filling it. When a new word rushes in, notice it, and set it down.

1246.title: Maximus the Confessor
1246.hook: punished, tradition says, for teaching that Christ had a human will; he saw the whole cosmos as a liturgy
1246.howItsDone: Orthodox and Catholic Christians honor Maximus as a saint; Christians of different churches pray Jesus's words from Gethsemane, "not my will, but thine," when facing a hard choice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ladder of names: name God going down, take the names off going up. Your line was beyond every name.

Night, on the Mount of Olives. Jesus walks about a stone's throw from his friends and kneels down to pray. Luke gives the words: "Father, if thou be willing, remove this cup from me: nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done." Not my will. So he had one. A monk named Maximus read that line and wouldn't let it go, and tradition says it cost him dearly. He's remembered as the Confessor.

In Maximus's day, a teaching was spreading that Christ had only one will. It was meant to keep the peace between quarreling churches. Maximus said no. If the Son of God became fully human, he became human all the way down, and a human being has a human will. In the garden we hear that will speak: remove this cup. Then we hear it freely say yes: not my will, but thine. That yes, Maximus taught, is where a human will is healed, not erased. Tradition says he was put on trial, refused to back down, and was punished with terrible cruelty and sent into exile. So he's called Confessor: someone who suffered for confessing the faith. And he saw a larger picture. Every created thing, he taught, has its own word, its own reason for being, from the one Word who made it: a stone, a sparrow, a person. All of it is meant to be gathered back to God. Ephesians speaks of God gathering "together in one all things in Christ." Maximus saw the church at worship as a small model of that whole, and the whole world as a kind of worship. Some readers sum up his vision as a cosmic liturgy. That closes a week of great thinkers: Athanasius on why the Word became flesh, the Cappadocians' three and one, Augustine's restless heart and his picture of love, Boethius and the wheel, Dionysius and the ladder of names. And now Maximus: a human will saying yes, inside a universe at prayer.

Notice one thing you want badly right now, big or small, and name it plainly; Jesus didn't pretend in the garden. If you pray, you can say his words from Luke: not my will, but thine, be done. If you don't, hold the wanting with an open hand instead of a fist, and breathe around it.
Maximus the Confessor. A monk who taught that Christ had a real human will that freely said yes, and who saw all creation gathered into worship.
Your line: a cosmic liturgy. In Maximus's eyes, even a sparrow belongs to the worship. Go gently.

fork.setup: you're Maximus. a teaching that Christ had only one will is meant to keep the peace between churches. what do you do?
options: go along with it for the sake of peace.
say no: a fully human Christ had a human will.
stay silent and stay safe.
fork.reveal: Maximus refused. tradition says he was tried, punished with cruelty, and exiled for it, which is why the church calls him Confessor.

original.note: Greek: word, reason. Maximus taught that each created thing has its own logos from the one Logos, the Word.

trapdoor: what you thought: if Jesus is God, he couldn't have wanted anything different.
what it means: Maximus taught Christ had a real human will, which said remove this cup, then freely said not my will, but thine.
what a scholar hears: two wills in one person, and a cosmos where every thing's own logos is gathered back to the Logos.
guess: a monk who held that Christ had a human will
a monk who heard confessions for a whole city
an emperor who settled a quarrel between churches

chat.says: Why did Maximus care whether Jesus had a human will? Isn't that splitting hairs?
options: He said if the Son became fully human, he had a human will, which freely said yes.
He said Jesus had no will of his own, so the garden prayer was only for show.
He said Jesus's human will fought God's to the end and never really said yes.
chat.meaning: For Maximus, being fully human means having a human will. In the garden that will speaks, then freely says yes: healed, not erased.

Mount of Olives.meaning: the hill where Jesus prayed on his last night
